summary: Adds message relay intermediaries to MSRP, which was originally designed for direct peer-to-peer exchanges. The document describes the extensions needed to use relays. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4976 extends MSRP so clients can send messages through one or more relay servers. Clients authenticate to each relay and receive a private routing URI, which lets relays check that they are forwarding messages for an authorized client.

questions: how do relays work with msrp
what is the use-path header in msrp
how do msrp relays avoid being open relays
subtitle: How MSRP messages travel through authorized relay servers.

tldr.problem: MSRP was designed for direct exchanges, but clients may need intermediaries to cross network boundaries or apply policy. Those intermediaries must not become open relays for unsolicited traffic.
tldr.mechanism: A client authenticates to a relay with an AUTH request over TLS and HTTP Digest, then receives a secret URI for routing. A relay forwards only messages whose path contains a URI it issued and whose direction matches the authorized client or relay.
tldr.outcome: Clients can use one or more relays, and relays can forward message chunks and reports between them. RFC 4976 is updated by RFC 7977, RFC 8553 and RFC 8996.

today: RFC 4976 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 7977, RFC 8553 and RFC 8996. Read it together with those updates.

sections.title: Why MSRP Uses Relays
sections.content:
MSRP carries a session of messages directly between clients. RFC 4976 adds relays for cases where clients cannot connect directly or where an intermediary must enforce policy. A path may include any number of relays under different administrative control.

The design keeps direct client-to-client operation available and allows a client to choose the relays used on its behalf. It aims to prevent unsolicited messages, open relays and denial-of-service amplification, while supporting binary content and large transfers.

Clients that accept new TCP connections directly do not need new functionality to communicate through relays. Relays may share connections among sessions and can split or combine message chunks during forwarding.
sections.plainLanguage: MSRP clients can send messages directly or route them through relay servers. Each client chooses the relays it needs and must authenticate before a relay forwards its traffic.

sections.title: Paths, Hops and Acknowledgements
sections.content:
The To-Path header lists the remaining destinations, with the next hop first and the final recipient last. The From-Path header records the route back to the original sender. When a relay forwards a request, it removes its URI from the start of To-Path and adds that URI to the start of From-Path.

A portion of a complete message carried in one SEND request is a chunk. By default, a SEND is acknowledged at each hop; other requests are acknowledged end to end. A REPORT request is never acknowledged.

Relays may split or combine chunks and must send the resulting chunks in order. They must not combine chunks with different Message-ID values. A recipient can send REPORT requests with delivery status back along the reverse path.
sections.plainLanguage: Each request lists where it still needs to go and keeps a separate list for the return route. A relay can acknowledge receipt before forwarding a message chunk to the next hop.

sections.title: Authenticating with AUTH
sections.content:
A client opens a TLS connection to its first relay, checks that the relay certificate matches the intended hostname, and sends an AUTH request. A relay challenges an initial request with 401 Unauthorized and a WWW-Authenticate header. The client retries with credentials in an Authorization header using HTTP Digest authentication.

A successful response includes a Use-Path header containing one or more relay URIs and an Expires value specifying how long those URIs remain valid. A URI must include a fully qualified domain name and an explicit port. A relay may reject an unacceptable requested lifetime with a 423 response and a Min-Expires or Max-Expires header.

When several relays are used, the client authenticates to each one, routing later AUTH requests through relays already authorized. The URI is a secret routing token: clients must not reuse the same URI for multiple sessions or expose it to people outside the session.
sections.plainLanguage: A client proves its identity to a relay and receives a temporary URI for routing messages. The URI acts as a secret, so the client must keep it private and use a different one for each session.

sections.title: Forwarding Messages and Reports
sections.content:
Before forwarding a request, a relay checks that the first To-Path URI is one it issued. It also checks that the request is moving toward or coming from the client or relay authorized to use that URI. The relay creates a new transaction identifier when needed to avoid conflicts on a connection.

For a SEND with Failure-Report: yes, the relay immediately acknowledges receipt to the previous hop. That response means only that the relay received the chunk, not that it reached the next hop. Once the final byte has been sent onward, the relay starts a timer; if no response arrives within 30 seconds, it sends the original sender a REPORT with status 408.

Relays may re-chunk messages and should update Byte-Range when they know the range being sent. They must not combine SEND chunks with different Message-ID values. Responses use existing connections; if the connection has closed, the relay silently discards the response.
sections.plainLanguage: A relay checks that a message uses a routing URI it issued before sending the message onward. If a requested next-hop confirmation does not arrive within 30 seconds, the relay reports a timeout to the sender.

sections.title: Connections and Finding Relays
sections.content:
Clients reuse a suitable active connection to the next hop or open a new one when needed. A client should keep a relay connection open until no sessions have used it for a locally chosen period; the defaults are 5 minutes for foreign relays and one hour for the client's own relays.

A relay waits up to 30 seconds for an MSRP request after a connection is established and closes the connection if none arrives. Relays reuse existing connections first and may open new ones, typically to other relays. Responses can be sent only on existing connections.

Relay discovery uses the URI and DNS records. When a relay URI has no port, clients look up the _msrps._tcp service and may fall back to an address lookup using port 2855. AUTH requests are sent only over TLS.
sections.plainLanguage: Clients and relays reuse open connections when possible and close idle connections after a period of time. A relay URI and DNS records tell a client how to find the next relay.

sections.title: Security and Relay Authorization
sections.content:
Clients and relays must implement TLS, and clients must authenticate relay certificates. A client authenticates to a relay with Digest authentication; relay-to-relay connections use mutual TLS. The relay's certificate name must match the hostname in its URI.

A relay's URI must contain at least 64 bits of cryptographically random material. A relay discards a request that uses an invalid URI. It forwards messages only to or from the client associated with the URI, which limits the URI's use to that client's authorized route.

Relays are trusted nodes: a relay on the path can forge, alter or copy messages. The RFC notes that S/MIME signatures and encryption can help detect or limit some changes, but they do not remove the need to trust relays.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS protects connections, while authentication checks clients and neighboring relays. A relay's private URI limits who can send through it, but each relay can still inspect or change messages that pass through it.
